papers.titleEn: Versatile Acetyl-Functionalized Phenothiazine Self-Assembled Monolayers for Efficient Perovskite and Organic Solar Cells
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT The development of versatile, stable, and cost‐effective hole‐transport layers (HTLs) is essential for advancing next‐generation photovoltaic technologies. Herein, we report a series of phenothiazine‐based self‐assembled monolayers (SAMs) as HTLs for perovskite and organic solar cells. By systematically tuning the substituents, including unsubstituted phenothiazine (PTZ), dibromo‐PTZ (PTZ‐diBr), and diacetyl‐PTZ (PTZ‐diACE), we achieve control over interfacial energetics and surface properties. The dual coordination sites of carbonyl groups and sulfur in PTZ‐diACE provide Lewis basic sites that coordinate undercoordinated Pb 2 + ions, facilitating passivation at the buried HTL/perovskite interface. Additionally, polar acetyl groups induce interfacial dipoles that reinforce the built‐in electric field, promoting efficient hole extraction. Among the series, PTZ‐diACE exhibits superior film formation, a deeper HOMO level, and stronger interfacial interactions, resulting in enhanced charge extraction and suppressed nonradiative recombination. Consequently, inverted perovskite solar cells employing PTZ‐diACE achieve a power‐conversion efficiency (PCE) of 25.5% with excellent operational stability, retaining 93% of its initial efficiency after 500 h under the ISOS‐D‐2I protocol. These advantages extend to organic solar cells, where PTZ‐diACE delivers a PCE of 20.4% in D18:L8BO devices and demonstrates compatibility across multiple active layers. This study demonstrates phenothiazine‐based SAMs as HTLs and provides design guidelines for efficient, stable interfacial materials.
papers.filename: Joo Hyun Kim, Adv. Energy Mater., 2026, Versatile Acetyl-Functionalized Phenothiazine Self-Assembled Monolayers for Efficient Perovskite and Organic Solar Cells

papers.titleEn: Steric Ligand Engineering and Flow Crystallization Enable Stable Cyan CsPbBr 3 Nanocrystals for Micro-LED Color Conversion
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Although cyan‐emitting perovskite nanocrystals (NCs) are attractive for emerging micro‐light‐emitting diode (micro‐LED) displays, their practical deployment remains limited by their inadequate colloidal stability, insufficient process reproducibility, and unstable color‐conversion performance. Herein, we report a synergistic strategy that integrates steric ligand engineering with continuous flow crystallization control to produce stable cyan‐emitting CsPbBr 3 NCs. By screening protonic ligands with distinct acidities and anchoring groups, we identified dodecylbenzenesulfonic acid (DBSA) as an effective ligand that simultaneously regulates crystal growth and passivates surface defects. The further optimization of DBSA loading, Cs: Pb precursor flow rate ratio, and reaction temperature yielded DBSA–CsPbBr 3 NCs with an emission peak at 493 nm and an average photoluminescence quantum yield of 83.6 ± 2.0% across three independent syntheses. Structural and spectroscopic analyses indicate that DBSA predominantly interacts with Pb‐related surface sites, suppresses trap‐assisted relaxation, and substantially improves ambient and thermal stability. We subsequently integrated the optimized NCs into patterned GaN microstructures and silicone/PMMA composite films, obtaining cyan emission at 497–498 nm, prolonged solid‐state lifetime, and a color‐conversion efficiency of 33%. Our results establish a structure–process–property–device framework for cyan perovskite NCs and highlight the potential of flow‐enabled steric ligand engineering for micro‐LED color conversion.
papers.filename: Ru‐Shi Liu, Small, 2026, Steric Ligand Engineering and Flow Crystallization Enable Stable Cyan CsPbBr 3 Nanocrystals for Micro-LED Color Conversion

papers.titleEn: Gelatin-itaconate enables room-temperature extrusion-based 3D printing as a high-performance, sustainable alternative to GelMA
papers.abstract: Gelatin methacrylate (GelMA) is a widely used photocrosslinkable biomaterial for tissue engineering and biofabrication; however, its synthesis relies on petroleum-derived methacrylic anhydride/acid, and its precursor formulations generally require low-temperature processing to achieve sufficient printability. Here, we present gelatin–itaconate (GelIA), synthesized using bio-based itaconic acid, as a sustainable alternative to GelMA for room-temperature extrusion-based 3D printing. To isolate the influence of functional-group chemistry, GelIA and GelMA were synthesized with equivalent degrees of functionalization (36–38%) and systematically characterized by TNBS assay, ¹H NMR, FTIR, SEM, rheology, in situ photorheology, compression testing, swelling, enzymatic degradation, tissue adhesion, and printability evaluation. Compared with GelMA, GelIA exhibited higher precursor viscosity, pronounced shear-thinning behavior, improved structural recovery, and enabled stable extrusion-based 3D printing at 21–23 °C using only 5% (w/v) polymer, whereas GelMA with the same degree of functionalization was not printable under identical conditions. Following photocrosslinking, GelIA formed a more interconnected hydrogel network with enhanced viscoelastic properties, higher effective crosslink density, improved compressive properties, superior tissue adhesion, and greater structural integrity, resulting in enhanced stress-relaxation behavior. Despite exhibiting a higher swelling capacity, GelIA degraded more slowly than GelMA, indicating improved hydrogel stability. These findings validate our hypothesis that the additional carboxylic acid functionality of bio-based itaconate strengthens intermolecular interactions within the gelatin network, thereby improving both precursor rheology and hydrogel performance without increasing polymer concentration. Collectively, GelIA represents not only a sustainable, high-performance alternative to GelMA but also demonstrates how rational functional-group engineering can be exploited to regulate intermolecular interactions, enabling next-generation photocrosslinkable bioinks for room-temperature biofabrication and tissue engineering.
papers.filename: Vijay Singh Parihar, Chem. Eng. J., 2026, Gelatin-itaconate enables room-temperature extrusion-based 3D printing as a high-performance, sustainable alternative to GelMA
